studyPages.title: Why Materials Move in Cells
studyPages.body:
WHY MATERIALS MOVE IN CELLS
====

WHAT YOU WILL LEARN
----
• Explain why materials move in cells in your own words.
• Give a real Kenyan example that shows why materials move in cells.
• Avoid a common mistake learners make about why materials move in cells.

INTRODUCTION
----
Around a hardware shop in Nakuru, learners meet science ideas without opening a textbook. 2.2 Movement of Material in and Out of the Cell. This page explains why materials move in cells so you can recognise it, name it correctly, and use it safely.

MAIN NOTES
----
• 2.2 Movement of Material in and Out of the Cell.
• Diffusion is defined as the movement of molecules from a region of high concentratio to a region of low concentratio.
• Cells and unicellular organisms such as amoeba get rid of waste substance through diffusion.
• Gaseous exchange is the process through which gases are transferred across cell membrane to either enter or leave the blood. This process is done by diffusion in human beings in the alveoli in lungs. Oxygen gas moves from alveoli where is it is highly concentrated to the blood capillaries where it is lowly concentrated.
• Temperature-high temperature increases energy and therefore faster movement of molecules. This increases the rate of diffusion.
• What can we compare the visking tubing with in living cells?.
• Osmosis is the random movement of water (solvent) molecules from there they are more to where they are less through a semi-permeable membrane.

The learner then explains the science in their own words, checks a symbol or formula if one applies (for example H₂O, NaCl, Fe, or P = F / A), and writes a short conclusion that matches the definition on this page.

studyPages.title: Solutes Solvents and Solutions
studyPages.body:
SOLUTES SOLVENTS AND SOLUTIONS
====

WHAT YOU WILL LEARN
----
• Explain solutes solvents and solutions in your own words.
• Give a real Kenyan example that shows solutes solvents and solutions.
• Avoid a common mistake learners make about solutes solvents and solutions.

INTRODUCTION
----
Around a kitchen in Kisumu, learners meet science ideas without opening a textbook. When a solid is dissolved in a liquid, we get a solution formed. This page explains solutes solvents and solutions so you can recognise it, name it correctly, and use it safely.

MAIN NOTES
----
• A solute is the substance that dissolves, for example sugar or salt.
• A solvent is the liquid that does the dissolving. Water is the most common solvent in school experiments and in the body.
• A solution is the mixture formed when the solute dissolves completely in the solvent.
• A concentrated solution has a lot of solute compared with solvent. A dilute solution has little solute compared with solvent.

WORKED EXAMPLE
----
Tonny stirs three spoons of sugar into a glass of water at a kitchen in Kisumu. Sugar is the solute, water is the solvent, and the sweet liquid is the solution. When he adds only half a spoon to another glass, that tea is more dilute. Same solute and solvent — different concentration.

IN EVERYDAY LIFE
----
In everyday life around a kitchen in Kisumu, you can spot solutes solvents and solutions when you look carefully at materials, heat, food, tools, or living things. Safety tip: follow teacher and lab rules, protect your eyes when heating, never taste unknown chemicals, and raise the alarm early if you see smoke or fire.

DIFFUSION DEFINED
====

WHAT YOU WILL LEARN
----
• Explain diffusion defined in your own words.
• Give a real Kenyan example that shows diffusion defined.

INTRODUCTION
----
Around a shamba in Nyeri, learners meet science ideas without opening a textbook. Experiment demonstrating diffusion in gases. This page explains diffusion defined so you can recognise it, name it correctly, and use it safely.

MAIN NOTES
----
• Diffusion is the net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration.
• It happens in gases and liquids without anyone stirring.
• Perfume opened in one corner of a classroom is soon smelled elsewhere because perfume particles diffuse through air.
• A drop of ink in still water spreads as ink particles diffuse through the water.

• After a few minutes, the ink or dye spread throughout the water in the beaker.

• Diffusion distance- rate of diffusion depends on distance that particles have to travel in order to be evenly distributed within available space.
